title: Diwan Todar Mal
hook: tradition says he bought land for the children's cremation by covering it with gold coins

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nawab of Malerkotla, who protested when the Guru's youngest sons were sentenced. Your line was he spoke up. Where did a word from you count for someone? Today, the same sorrow, and a man who answered it with gold. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

Sirhind, in winter. The sentence has been carried out. The Guru's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, are dead, and tradition says their grandmother, Mata Gujri, died in the cold tower where she was held. Now there is one more thing a family is owed: a cremation. That takes ground. And the ground around Sirhind belongs to people who are afraid of the governor. Nobody wants to be the one who helped. Then a man of the town with wealth and position steps forward and asks to buy a plot. Tradition says the owner named a price meant to make him leave. Today: Diwan Todar Mal.
screen: `SIRHIND, IN WINTER.` → `NOBODY WANTS TO HELP.` → `A PRICE MEANT TO SEND HIM AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here is the price, as tradition tells it. The owner said he would sell only as much ground as Todar Mal could cover with gold coins. Some tellings go further: the coins had to stand on their edges, side by side, so the cost would be far higher than coins laid flat. Either way, it was an outrageous demand. And Todar Mal didn't bargain. He brought the gold, covered the ground, and bought it. Mata Gujri and the two boys were cremated there with dignity. Sikhs remember the spot at Fatehgarh Sahib, where a gurdwara now stands, and they gather there in winter to remember the children. Three things in this story are worth slowing down for. First, who he was. Todar Mal was not a Sikh soldier or a member of the Guru's household. Sikh tradition remembers him as a Hindu of Sirhind, a man with a position and wealth to lose. He risked both. Second, who the gift was for. A gift usually brings some thanks back. This gift went to people who could never repay it, a grandmother and two children who had already died. Third, what the gold bought. Not a monument, not a statement, just enough ground to do what a family is owed. Grief, in this story, becomes something practical. Nobody could undo the sentence. Todar Mal did the one thing still left to do, and he did it at full price. Sikhs remember his name with deep gratitude. His story is a reminder, as Sikhs tell it, that the person who stands closest in the hardest hour can be a neighbor with a purse and a conscience.
screen: `THE GROUND, COVERED IN GOLD.` · `NOT A SIKH, AND HE RISKED IT ALL.` · `A GIFT NOBODY COULD REPAY.` · `THE ONE THING STILL LEFT TO DO.` · then, large: `GOLD FOR THE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give generously for a good cause. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one cause that serves people who can't pay you back. A food bank. A hospice. A family on your street going through a loss. A gurdwara's langar. Pick one. Now decide on one gift, money, time or something you own, and notice the urge to bargain it down. Let the first, larger number stand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out while you hold that cause in mind. The bell holds the time.
Diwan Todar Mal. The man of Sirhind who, tradition says, covered the ground in gold so Mata Gujri and the Guru's youngest sons could be cremated. Today's word.
Your line: gold for the children. Today, give the gift you chose in the sit, at the first number, without haggling with yourself. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Diwan Todar Mal at Fatehgarh Sahib, where Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade were cremated, and gather there in winter to honor the children and those who stood by them.
